newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to shed light on domestic oil product trade.
newsitem.headline: Japan to shed light on domestic oil product trade.

text.p: A government advisory panel has recommended that a greater degree of openness be imposed on Japan's covert inter-dealer oil product market, a government official said on Wednesday.

"The panel believes, in a sense, that the closed inter-dealer market should come out of the darkness into the brighter world," the official for the Ministry of International Trade and Industry's Agency of Natural Resources and Energy said.
About three to five percent of Japanese oil products are distributed through the inter-dealer market, traders said.
Although the inter-dealer market functions as an integral part of the the domestic oil industry, it has been criticised for unclear trading practices, traders said.
Japan's refiners have traditionally supplied oil products such as gasoline, gas oil, and kerosene only to the regional wholesalers and petrol stations belonging to their own distribution groups.

Any surplus material refiners are unable to sell within their own distribution networks are quietly passed on to domestic oil dealers, who then sell the material as "non-brand" products to other service stations at a discount price.

Refiners also use this covert market to procure spot cargoes when customer demand exceeds their production. The oil industry has been reluctant to acknowledge the inter-dealer market publicly, partly in order to preserve consumer confidence that products sold under the brand name of a particular retail outlet are indeed produced by that outlet's parent refiner, traders say.
But traders also point out that public knowledge of the inter-dealer trade, which allows retailers to secure bargain wholesale prices, would likely act to deflate end-user price levels at the pump.
In order to transform the exclusive inter-dealer market into a legitimate spot market, the government has proposed the introduction of price assessments by a neutral "third party".
Officials say discussions are still proceeding as to whether the independent price setter would be an existing news service or a separate government panel.
Some traders also said that the initiative goes hand in hand with government efforts to encourage a Tokyo-based oil futures market.
"Japan must have a liquid and transparent spot market for products if it is to successfully establish an oil futures market," said one trader.
The Tokyo Commodities Exchange plans to launch either a crude oil or gasoline futures contract in April 1999.
